x.title: Radial Acceleration Relation in Rotationally Supported Galaxies
x.abstract: We report a correlation between the radial acceleration traced by rotation curves and that predicted by the observed distribution of baryons. The same relation is followed by 2693 points in 153 galaxies with very different morphologies, masses, sizes, and gas fractions. The correlation persists even when dark matter dominates. Consequently, the dark matter contribution is fully specified by that of the baryons. The observed scatter is small and largely dominated by observational uncertainties. This radial acceleration relation is tantamount to a natural law for rotating galaxies.

tag.main_claim: McGaugh et al. show that a universal radial acceleration relation exists across 153 rotationally supported galaxies, in which the total acceleration (including the dark matter contribution) is fully specified by the baryonic acceleration, constituting a natural law for rotating galaxies.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper explicitly frames the result in terms of dark matter's contribution being specified by baryons (P1), and the predicted acceleration from the observed baryonic distribution is computed using Newtonian dynamics (P2). If dark matter does not exist or Newtonian dynamics break down at low accelerations, the paper's interpretation of the relation as a dark-matter-contribution regularity would be undercut.
tag.evidence_quote: The correlation persists even when dark matter dominates. Consequently, the dark matter contribution is fully specified by that of the baryons.

y.title: Novel Test of Modified Newtonian Dynamics with Gas Rich Galaxies
y.abstract: The current cosmological paradigm, the cold dark matter model with a cosmological constant, requires that the mass-energy of the Universe be dominated by invisible components: dark matter and dark energy. An alternative to these dark components is that the law of gravity be modified on the relevant scales. A test of these ideas is provided by the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation (BTFR), an empirical relation between the observed mass of a galaxy and its rotation velocity. Here, I report a test using gas rich galaxies for which both axes of the BTFR can be measured independently of the theories being tested and without the systematic uncertainty in stellar mass that affects the same test with star dominated spirals. The data fall precisely where predicted a priori by the modified Newtonian dynamics. The scatter in the BTFR is attributable entirely to observational uncertainty, consistent with a single effective force law.

tag.main_claim: McGaugh shows that gas-rich galaxies fall precisely on the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation with scatter attributable entirely to observational uncertainty, consistent with a single effective force law governing galaxy dynamics.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim depends on MOND's modified force law (Q2) producing a specific, a priori prediction for the BTFR normalization and slope (Q3). If Newtonian dynamics held at low accelerations, or if the BTFR emerged from galaxy formation physics rather than a fundamental force law, MOND's prediction would not be the thing being validated.
tag.evidence_quote: The data fall precisely where predicted a priori by the modified Newtonian dynamics. The scatter in the BTFR is attributable entirely to observational uncertainty, consistent with a single effective force law.

judge.conjunction: McGaugh and collaborators have established universal scaling relations in galaxy dynamics—the radial acceleration relation across 153 galaxies [x] and the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation in gas-rich galaxies [y]—showing that the total dynamical mass is fully specified by baryons, consistent with a single effective force law.
judge.x_background_statement: The observed acceleration g_obs = v²/r is computed from rotation curves using Newtonian kinematics, and the baryonic acceleration g_bar is computed from the observed baryon distribution using Newtonian gravity; the residual (g_obs − g_bar) is attributed to dark matter, and the tight correlation between g_obs and g_bar is an empirical regularity within this Newtonian-plus-dark-matter framework.
judge.y_background_statement: Below the characteristic acceleration a0, Newtonian dynamics break down and galaxy dynamics are governed by a single modified force law, so the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation follows directly from this modified force law rather than from Newtonian gravity plus dark matter.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P2 asserts that Newtonian dynamics hold at very low accelerations, requiring dark matter to explain the mass discrepancy. Q2 asserts that Newtonian dynamics break down below a0, so the same discrepancy reflects modified gravity with no need for dark matter. The two positions on whether Newtonian dynamics are valid at low accelerations are mutually exclusive.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Dark matter in galaxies follows a single effective force law, as evidenced by both the radial acceleration relation and the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation.
judge.notes: Both papers are by McGaugh, who uses empirical scaling relations to probe the dark-matter-vs-MOND tension. Paper x operates within the Lambda-CDM framework: it explicitly references dark matter dominating at large radii and decomposes acceleration into baryonic and dark matter components using Newtonian dynamics (P2). Paper y explicitly frames its result as a test of MOND and concludes consistency with 'a single effective force law,' directly invoking Q2. A literature-review writer combining these without flagging the theoretical tension would implicitly suggest that dark matter behaves as if governed by a modified force law—a claim Lambda-CDM rejects (the RAR emerges from galaxy formation/feedback, not a force law) and MOND also rejects (there is no dark matter). Human verifier should confirm that the RAR paper's use of Newtonian dynamics to compute both g_obs and g_bar constitutes a genuine dependence on P2 rather than a purely kinematic measurement independent of dynamical theory.

x.title: The Intrinsic Scatter of the Radial Acceleration Relation*
x.abstract: Abstract We present a detailed Monte Carlo model of observational errors in observed galaxy scaling relations to recover the intrinsic (cosmic) scatter driven by galaxy formation and evolution processes. We apply our method to the stellar radial acceleration relation (RAR), which compares the local observed radial acceleration to the local Newtonian radial acceleration computed from the stellar mass distribution. The stellar and baryonic RAR are known to exhibit similar scatter. Lelli+2017 (L17) studied the baryonic RAR using a sample of 153 spiral galaxies and inferred a negligible intrinsic scatter. If true, a small scatter might challenge the ΛCDM galaxy formation paradigm, possibly favoring a modified Newtonian dynamics interpretation. The intrinsic scatter of the baryonic RAR is predicted by modern ΛCDM simulations to be ∼0.06–0.08 dex, contrasting with the null value reported by L17. We have assembled a catalog of structural properties with over 2500 spiral galaxies from six deep imaging and spectroscopic surveys (called the “Photometry and Rotation curve OBservations from Extragalactic Surveys”) to quantify the intrinsic scatter of the stellar RAR and other scaling relations. The stellar RAR for our full sample has a median observed scatter of 0.17 dex. We use our Monte Carlo method, which accounts for all major sources of measurement uncertainty, to infer a contribution of 0.12 dex from the observational errors. The intrinsic scatter of the stellar RAR is thus estimated to be 0.11 ± 0.02 dex, in agreement with, though slightly greater than, current ΛCDM predictions.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that the intrinsic scatter of the radial acceleration relation is ~0.11 dex, consistent with ΛCDM predictions of non-negligible scatter arising from galaxy formation processes.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim that the RAR has non-negligible intrinsic scatter consistent with ΛCDM depends on P3, which holds that galaxy scaling relations emerge from galaxy formation and feedback rather than being fundamental laws. If the RAR were a fundamental law (as Q3 asserts), negligible scatter would be expected, and the ΛCDM simulation predictions of 0.06–0.08 dex scatter would not apply.
tag.evidence_quote: The intrinsic scatter of the baryonic RAR is predicted by modern ΛCDM simulations to be ∼0.06–0.08 dex, contrasting with the null value reported by L17. ... The intrinsic scatter of the stellar RAR is thus estimated to be 0.11 ± 0.02 dex, in agreement with, though slightly greater than, current ΛCDM predictions.

y.title: Fitting the radial acceleration relation to individual SPARC galaxies
y.abstract: Galaxies follow a tight radial acceleration relation (RAR): the acceleration observed at every radius correlates with that expected from the distribution of baryons. We use the Markov chain Monte Carlo method to fit the mean RAR to 175 individual galaxies in the SPARC database, marginalizing over stellar mass-to-light ratio (ϒ⋆), galaxy distance, and disk inclination. Acceptable fits with astrophysically reasonable parameters are found for the vast majority of galaxies. The residuals around these fits have an rms scatter of only 0.057 dex (~13%). This is in agreement with the predictions of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND). We further consider a generalized version of the RAR that, unlike MOND, permits galaxy-to-galaxy variation in the critical acceleration scale. The fits are not improved with this additional freedom: there is no credible indication of variation in the critical acceleration scale. The data are consistent with the action of a single effective force law. The apparent universality of the acceleration scale and the small residual scatter are key to understanding galaxies.

tag.main_claim: The radial acceleration relation across 175 SPARC galaxies shows a universal critical acceleration scale with only ~13% residual scatter, consistent with a single effective force law as predicted by MOND.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's claim that the RAR reflects a single effective force law with a universal critical acceleration scale directly invokes MOND's core tenets: that baryons alone explain galaxy dynamics (Q1), that dynamics break down below a characteristic acceleration a0 (Q2), and that scaling relations like the RAR follow directly from the force law rather than from galaxy formation (Q3). If any of these were rejected—for instance, if the RAR arose from dark matter halo physics (P3) rather than a fundamental force law—the paper's central interpretive conclusion would be undercut.

judge.conjunction: The radial acceleration relation has been established as a universal law across 153 galaxies, with the dark matter contribution fully specified by baryons [x], and subsequent fitting to 175 SPARC galaxies confirmed a universal critical acceleration scale with only ~13% residual scatter, consistent with a single effective force law as predicted by MOND [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Most matter in the universe is non-baryonic dark matter, so the total acceleration in galaxies includes a dominant dark matter contribution that the RAR shows is fully specified by the baryonic distribution.
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy dynamics are explained by baryonic matter alone without dark matter, so the RAR's universal acceleration scale reflects a single modified force law rather than a dark-matter halo relation.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P1 asserts that non-baryonic dark matter exists and dominates galactic mass budgets, while Q1 asserts that no dark matter is needed and galaxy dynamics are explained by baryons alone under modified gravity. Both cannot hold: either the extra mass is non-baryonic dark matter or it is not there at all.
judge.orphan_conclusion: The radial acceleration relation demonstrates that the dark matter contribution to galactic dynamics is set by baryons through a single modified force law—implying that dark matter exists and is governed by MOND-like dynamics simultaneously. ΛCDM rejects the force-law interpretation (P3 attributes the RAR to galaxy formation and feedback, not a fundamental law), and MOND rejects the existence of dark matter (Q1).
judge.notes: Both papers study the same relation (RAR) in the same class of objects (rotationally supported galaxies in SPARC), so there is no regime separation that licenses combining the dark-matter interpretation with the MOND interpretation. A human verifier should confirm that Paper x (McGaugh et al. 2016) genuinely frames the RAR within the dark-matter paradigm—it does, by explicitly stating 'the dark matter contribution is fully specified by that of the baryons'—and that Paper y (Li et al. 2018) genuinely frames it within MOND—it does, by stating 'in agreement with the predictions of modified Newtonian dynamics' and 'consistent with the action of a single effective force law.' The key subtlety: McGaugh is an author on both papers, and the RAR community itself straddles both frameworks, which makes the surface consistency especially natural and the hidden conflict especially easy to overlook in a literature review.

x.title: Feedback and the fundamental line of low-luminosity low-surface-brightness/dwarf galaxies
x.abstract: We study in simple terms the role of feedback in establishing the scaling relations of low-surface-brightness (LSB) and dwarf galaxies with stellar masses in the range 6 × 105≤M*≤ 3 × 1010 M⊙. These galaxies – as measured, for example, from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and in the Local Group – show tight correlations of internal velocity, metallicity and surface brightness (or radius) with M*. They define a fundamental line which distinguishes them from the brighter galaxies of high surface brightness and metallicity. The idealized model assumes spherical collapse of cold dark matter (CDM) haloes to virial equilibrium and angular momentum conservation. The relations for bright galaxies are reproduced by assuming that M* is a constant fraction of the halo mass M. The upper bound to the low-luminosity LSBs coincides with the virial velocity of haloes in which supernova feedback could significantly suppress star formation, V < 100 km s−1. We argue that the energy fed to the gas obeys ESN∝M* despite the radiative losses, and equate it with the binding energy of the gas to obtain M*/M∝V2. This idealized model provides surprisingly good fits to the scaling relations of low-luminosity LSBs and dwarfs, which indicates that supernova feedback had a primary role in determining the fundamental line. The apparent lower bound for galaxies at V∼ 10 km s−1 may be caused by the cooling barrier at T∼ 104 K. Some fraction of the dark haloes may show no stars as a result of complete gas removal, either by supernova winds from neighbouring galaxies or by radiative feedback after cosmological reionization at zion. Radiative feedback may also explain the distinction between dwarf spheroidals (dE) and irregulars (dI), where the dEs, typically of V≤ 30 km s−1, form stars before zion and are then cleaned out of gas, whereas the dIs, with V > 30 km s−1, retain gas-rich discs with feedback-regulated star formation.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that supernova feedback within CDM haloes is the primary mechanism establishing the fundamental line scaling relations of low-luminosity LSB and dwarf galaxies.
tag.dependence_explanation: The model explicitly assumes the existence of cold dark matter haloes (P1) as the gravitational scaffolding within which galaxies form, and the central claim that scaling relations arise from feedback processes rather than a fundamental law of dynamics directly instantiates P3. If dark matter haloes did not exist or if scaling relations were instead fundamental (as in MOND), the derivation would not hold.
tag.evidence_quote: The idealized model assumes spherical collapse of cold dark matter (CDM) haloes to virial equilibrium and angular momentum conservation. [...] This idealized model provides surprisingly good fits to the scaling relations of low-luminosity LSBs and dwarfs, which indicates that supernova feedback had a primary role in determining the fundamental line.

y.title: Modified Newtonian Dynamics as an Alternative to Dark Matter
y.abstract: ▪ Abstract Modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) is an empirically motivated modification of Newtonian gravity or inertia suggested by Milgrom as an alternative to cosmic dark matter. The basic idea is that at accelerations below a o ≈ 10 −8 cm/s 2 ≈ cH o /6 the effective gravitational attraction approaches [Formula: see text], where g n is the usual Newtonian acceleration. This simple algorithm yields flat rotation curves for spiral galaxies and a mass-rotation velocity relation of the form M ∝ V 4 that forms the basis for the observed luminosity–rotation velocity relation—the Tully-Fisher law. We review the phenomenological success of MOND on scales ranging from dwarf spheroidal galaxies to superclusters and demonstrate that the evidence for dark matter can be equally well interpreted as evidence for MOND. We discuss the possible physical basis for an acceleration-based modification of Newtonian dynamics as well as the extention of MOND to cosmology and structure formation.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that MOND successfully explains galaxy dynamics and scaling relations such as the Tully-Fisher law across scales from dwarf spheroidal galaxies to superclusters, providing an equally viable alternative interpretation of the evidence usually attributed to dark matter.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's central claim requires that Newtonian dynamics break down below a0 (Q2), that galaxy dynamics can be explained by baryons alone without dark matter (Q1), that scaling relations like the Tully-Fisher law follow directly from the modified force law (Q3), and that mass discrepancies up to supercluster scales reflect modified gravity rather than collisionless dark matter (Q4).
tag.evidence_quote: The basic idea is that at accelerations below a o ≈ 10 −8 cm/s 2 ≈ cH o /6 the effective gravitational attraction approaches [Formula: see text], where g n is the usual Newtonian acceleration. This simple algorithm yields flat rotation curves for spiral galaxies and a mass-rotation velocity relation of the form M ∝ V 4 that forms the basis for the observed luminosity–rotation velocity relation—the Tully-Fisher law. We review the phenomenological success of MOND on scales ranging from dwarf spheroidal galaxies to superclusters and demonstrate that the evidence for dark matter can be equally well interpreted as evidence for MOND.

judge.x_background_statement: Cold dark matter haloes exist and dominate the gravitational potential of galaxies, with baryonic stellar mass being a constant or feedback-regulated fraction of the halo mass M.
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy dynamics are explained entirely by baryonic matter through a modification of Newtonian dynamics below a characteristic acceleration a0, with no non-baryonic dark matter required.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: CDM haloes cannot both exist as the dominant mass component of galaxies (required by paper x's model, which assumes spherical collapse of CDM haloes to virial equilibrium) and be absent (required by MOND, which explicitly rejects dark matter and derives galaxy dynamics from baryons alone). The presence and absence of non-baryonic dark matter are mutually exclusive.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Galaxy scaling relations are overdetermined: they arise simultaneously from supernova feedback physics operating within dark matter haloes and from a fundamental modification to the gravitational force law, making the relations insensitive to whether dark matter actually exists.
judge.notes: Both papers address overlapping galaxy populations (dwarf/LSB galaxies appear in both). The orphan conclusion (dual overdetermination) is not endorsed by either framework: CDM does not invoke modified gravity, and MOND does not invoke dark matter haloes. Verify whether a reviewer might argue the papers address sufficiently distinct scaling relations to make the conjunction merely a survey of alternatives rather than a hidden conflict.

x.title: The baryonic Tully–Fisher relation in the simba simulation
x.abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate the Baryonic Tully–Fisher relation (BTFR) in the $(100\, h^{-1}{\rm Mpc})^3$simba hydrodynamical galaxy formation simulation together with a higher resolution $(25\, h^{-1}{\rm Mpc})^3$simba run, for over 10 000 disc-dominated, H i-rich galaxies. We generate simulated galaxy rotation curves from the mass distribution, which we show yields similar results to using the gas rotational velocities. From this, we measure the galaxy rotation velocity Vcirc using four metrics: $V_{\rm max}, V_{\rm flat}, V_{2R_e},$ and Vpolyex. We compare the predicted BTFR to the SPARC observational sample and find broad agreement. In detail, however, simba is biased towards higher Vcirc by up to 0.1 dex. We find evidence for the flattening of the BTFR in Vcirc > 300 km s−1 galaxies, in agreement with recent observational findings. simba’s rotation curves are more peaked for lower mass galaxies, in contrast with observations, suggesting overly bulge-dominated dwarf galaxies in our sample. We investigate for residuals around the BTFR versus H i mass, stellar mass, gas fraction, and specific star formation rate, which provide testable predictions for upcoming BTFR surveys. simba’s BTFR shows sub-optimal resolution mass convergence, with the higher resolution run lowering V in better agreement with data.

tag.main_claim: The SIMBA hydrodynamical simulation broadly reproduces the observed Baryonic Tully-Fisher relation, though with systematic biases, and predicts specific residual correlations with galaxy properties such as HI mass, stellar mass, gas fraction, and star formation rate.
tag.dependence_explanation: SIMBA is a dark-matter-based hydrodynamical simulation (P1) using Newtonian dynamics (P2), and the paper treats the BTFR as a relation that must emerge from galaxy formation and feedback processes rather than a fundamental law (P3). If dark matter did not exist, Newtonian dynamics broke down at low accelerations, or the BTFR were fundamental rather than emergent, the simulation approach and its predictions would be invalid.

We compare the predicted BTFR to the SPARC observational sample and find broad agreement.

y.title: Rotation Curves of Ursa Major Galaxies in the Context of Modified Newtonian Dynamics
y.abstract: This is the third in a series of papers in which spiral galaxy rotation curves are considered in the context of Milgrom's modified dynamics (MOND). The present sample of 30 objects is drawn from a complete sample of galaxies in the Ursa Major cluster, with photometric data from Tully et al. and 21 cm line data from Verheijen. The galaxies are roughly all at the same distance (15 to 16 Mpc). The radio observations are made with the Westerbork Synthesis Array, which means that the linear resolution of all rotation curves is comparable. The fitted M / L in the B -band correlates with B - V color in the sense predicted by population synthesis models. x.title: The core–cusp problem: a matter of perspective
x.abstract: The existence of two kinematically and chemically distinct stellar subpopulations in the Sculptor and Fornax dwarf galaxies offers the opportunity to constrain the density profile of their matter haloes by measuring the mass contained within the well-separated half-light radii of the two metallicity subpopulations. Walker and Peñarrubia have used this approach to argue that data for these galaxies are consistent with constant-density ‘cores’ in their inner regions and rule out ‘cuspy’ Navarro–Frenk–White (NFW) profiles with high statistical significance, particularly in the case of Sculptor. We test the validity of these claims using dwarf galaxies in the APOSTLE (A Project Of Simulating The Local Environment) Λ cold dark matter cosmological hydrodynamic simulations of analogues of the Local Group. These galaxies all have NFW dark matter density profiles and a subset of them develop two distinct metallicity subpopulations reminiscent of Sculptor and Fornax. We apply a method analogous to that of Walker and Peñarrubia to a sample of 50 simulated dwarfs and find that this procedure often leads to a statistically significant detection of a core in the profile when in reality there is a cusp. Although multiple factors contribute to these failures, the main cause is a violation of the assumption of spherical symmetry upon which the mass estimators are based. The stellar populations of the simulated dwarfs tend to be significantly elongated and, in several cases, the two metallicity populations have different asphericity and are misaligned. As a result, a wide range of slopes of the density profile are inferred depending on the angle from which the galaxy is viewed.

tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis presupposes that dwarf galaxies reside in non-baryonic dark matter haloes with NFW density profiles, as generated in ΛCDM cosmological simulations; rejecting P1 would remove the premise that such haloes exist and that the core–cusp problem is meaningful.

We apply a method analogous to that of Walker and Peñarrubia to a sample of 50 simulated dwarfs and find that this procedure often leads to a statistically significant detection of a core in the profile when in reality there is a cusp.

y.title: Galaxy rotation curves from general relativity with renormalization group corrections
y.abstract: We consider the application of quantum corrections computed using renormalization group arguments in the astrophysical domain and show that, for the most natural interpretation of the renormalization group scale parameter, a gravitational coupling parameter G varying 10 −7 of its value across a galaxy (which is roughly a variation of 10 −12 per light-year) is sufficient to generate galaxy rotation curves in agreement with the observations. The quality of the resulting fit is similar to the Isothermal profile quality once both the shape of the rotation curve and the mass-to-light ratios are considered for evaluation. In order to perform the analysis, we use recent high quality data from nine regular disk galaxies. For the sake of comparison, the same set of data is modeled also for the Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) and for the recently proposed Scalar Tensor Vector Gravity (STVG). At face value, the model based on quantum corrections clearly leads to better fits than these two alternative theories.

tag.dependence_explanation: The claim depends on Q1 because it requires that galaxy dynamics be explainable by baryonic matter alone without dark matter; if dark matter were necessary (P1), the varying-G fit would be superfluous and the rotation curves would be attributed to dark matter halos instead.
tag.evidence_quote: a gravitational coupling parameter G varying 10 −7 of its value across a galaxy (which is roughly a variation of 10 −12 per light-year) is sufficient to generate galaxy rotation curves in agreement with the observations.

If NFW dark matter haloes exist and dominate galaxy mass, then baryons alone cannot explain galaxy dynamics.

x.title: Incorporating baryon-driven contraction of dark matter halos in rotation curve fits
x.abstract: The condensation of baryons within a dark matter (DM) halo during galaxy formation should result in some contraction of the halo as the combined system settles into equilibrium. We quantify this effect on the cuspy primordial halos predicted by DM-only simulations for the baryon distributions observed in the galaxies of the SPARC database. We find that the DM halos of high surface brightness galaxies (with Σeff ≳ 100 L⊙ pc−2 at 3.6 μm) experience strong contraction. Halos become more cuspy as a result of compression: the inner DM density slope increases with the baryonic surface mass density. We iteratively fit rotation curves to find the balance between initial halo parameters (constrained by abundance matching), compression, and stellar mass-to-light ratio. The resulting fits often require lower stellar masses than expected for stellar populations, particularly in galaxies with bulges: stellar mass must be reduced to make room for the DM it compresses. This trade off between dark and luminous mass is reminiscent of the cusp-core problem in dwarf galaxies, but occurs in more massive systems: the present-epoch DM halos cannot follow from cuspy primordial halos unless (1) the stellar mass-to-light ratios are systematically smaller than expected from standard stellar population synthesis models, and/or (2) there is a net outward mass redistribution from the initial cusp, even in massive galaxies widely considered to be immune from such effects.

tag.main_claim: Kaplinghoff et al. show that incorporating baryon-driven contraction of dark matter halos in rotation curve fits of SPARC galaxies creates tension: either stellar mass-to-light ratios must be systematically lower than expected from stellar population synthesis, or there must be net outward mass redistribution from initial cusps, even in massive galaxies.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis assumes that galaxies are surrounded by non-baryonic dark matter halos (P1) and that rotation curves can be interpreted via Newtonian dynamics to infer the underlying mass distribution (P2). Without dark matter halos or under modified dynamics, the rotation-curve-fitting methodology and the resulting cusp-contraction tension would not arise.
tag.evidence_quote: The condensation of baryons within a dark matter (DM) halo during galaxy formation should result in some contraction of the halo as the combined system settles into equilibrium. We quantify this effect on the cuspy primordial halos predicted by DM-only simulations for the baryon distributions observed in the galaxies of the SPARC database.

y.title: Declining rotation curves of galaxies as a test of gravitational theory
y.abstract: Unlike Newtonian dynamics which is linear and obeys the strong equivalence principle, in any non-linear gravitation such as Milgromian dynamics (MOND), the strong version of the equivalence principle is violated and the gravitational dynamics of a system is influenced by the external gravitational field in which it is embedded. This so called external field effect (EFE) is one of the important implications of MOND and provides a special context to test Milgromian dynamics. Here, we study the rotation curves (RCs) of 18 spiral galaxies and find that their shapes constrain the EFE. We show that the EFE can successfully remedy the overestimation of rotation velocities in 80 per cent of the sample galaxies in Milgromian dynamics fits by decreasing the velocity in the outer part of the RCs. We compare the implied external field with the gravitational field for non-negligible nearby sources of each individual galaxy and find that in many cases it is compatible with the EFE within the uncertainties. We therefore argue that in the framework of Milgromian dynamics, one can constrain the gravitational field induced from the environment of galaxies using their RCs. We finally show that taking into account the EFE yields more realistic values for the stellar mass-to-light ratio in terms of stellar population synthesis than the ones implied without the EFE.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that MOND's external field effect can explain declining rotation curves in spiral galaxies and yields more realistic stellar mass-to-light ratios when included in MOND rotation curve fits.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim requires Q1 because the rotation curve fits assume baryonic matter alone with no dark matter, and Q2 because the external field effect arises specifically from the non-linearity of MOND's modified force law below the characteristic acceleration a0, which violates the strong equivalence principle.
tag.evidence_quote: Unlike Newtonian dynamics which is linear and obeys the strong equivalence principle, in any non-linear gravitation such as Milgromian dynamics (MOND), the strong version of the equivalence principle is violated and the gravitational dynamics of a system is influenced by the external gravitational field in which it is embedded. This so called external field effect (EFE) is one of the important implications of MOND and provides a special context to test Milgromian dynamics.

judge.conjunction: Recent studies of galaxy rotation curves show that baryon-driven contraction of dark matter halos creates tension with inferred stellar mass-to-light ratios in ΛCDM fits [x], and that MOND's external field effect yields more realistic stellar mass-to-light ratios when included in modified-gravity fits [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Dark matter halos exist and dominate galaxy mass budgets; rotation curves are decomposed into baryonic and dark matter components, and baryonic infall contracts the primordial dark matter halo.
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy dynamics are explained by baryonic matter alone within MOND, without dark matter; rotation curves are fit using modified gravity and its external field effect.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: Paper x's analysis requires dark matter halos to exist as the dominant mass component whose contraction must be modeled, while paper y's analysis requires that no dark matter exists and that galaxy dynamics arise purely from baryons under modified gravity. These assumptions are mutually exclusive: one cannot simultaneously fit a rotation curve with a contracting dark matter halo and with baryons-only modified gravity.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Both dark matter halo contraction and the MOND external field effect are real physical phenomena that must be accounted for when inferring reliable stellar mass-to-light ratios from rotation curve fits.
judge.notes: Both papers study the same class of galaxies (SPARC-type spirals) and both report effects on stellar mass-to-light ratios in rotation curve fits, making them appear complementary in a literature review. However, the physical mechanisms they describe are paradigm-specific: halo contraction only exists if dark matter halos are real (P1), and the EFE only exists if MOND's modified gravity replaces Newtonian dynamics without dark matter (Q1). Neither framework endorses the other's mechanism as a real physical effect. A reader combining both might wrongly conclude that both effects are established and must be jointly considered, when in fact each framework rejects the other's premise entirely.

x.title: The formation and evolution of low-surface-brightness galaxies
x.abstract: Our statistical understanding of galaxy evolution is fundamentally driven by objects that lie above the surface-brightness limits of current wide-area surveys (μ ∼ 23 mag arcsec−2). While both theory and small, deep surveys have hinted at a rich population of low-surface-brightness galaxies (LSBGs) fainter than these limits, their formation remains poorly understood. We use Horizon-AGN, a cosmological hydrodynamical simulation to study how LSBGs, and in particular the population of ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs; μ > 24.5 mag arcsec−2), form and evolve over time. For |$M_*\gt 10^{8}\, \mathrm{M}_{\odot }$|⁠, LSBGs contribute 47, 7, and 6 per cent of the local number, mass, and luminosity densities, respectively (∼85/11/10 per cent for |$M_*\gt 10^{7}\, \mathrm{M}_{\odot }$|⁠). Today’s LSBGs have similar dark-matter fractions and angular momenta to high-surface-brightness galaxies (HSBGs; μ < 23 mag arcsec−2), but larger effective radii (×2.5 for UDGs) and lower fractions of dense, star-forming gas (more than ×6 less in UDGs than HSBGs). LSBGs originate from the same progenitors as HSBGs at |$z$| > 2. However, LSBG progenitors form stars more rapidly at early epochs. The higher resultant rate of supernova-energy injection flattens their gas-density profiles, which, in turn, creates shallower stellar profiles that are more susceptible to tidal processes. After |$z$| ∼ 1, tidal perturbations broaden LSBG stellar distributions and heat their cold gas, creating the diffuse, largely gas-poor LSBGs seen today. In clusters, ram-pressure stripping provides an additional mechanism that assists in gas removal in LSBG progenitors. Our results offer insights into the formation of a galaxy population that is central to a complete understanding of galaxy evolution, and that will be a key topic of research using new and forthcoming deep-wide surveys.

tag.main_claim: Low-surface-brightness galaxies form through early rapid star formation whose supernova feedback flattens gas-density profiles, followed by tidal perturbations and ram-pressure stripping that produce the diffuse, gas-poor LSBGs observed today.
tag.dependence_explanation: The results derive from a cosmological hydrodynamical simulation (Horizon-AGN) built within the Lambda-CDM framework, and the paper explicitly reports dark-matter fractions for LSBGs. If dark matter did not exist (P1 rejected), the simulation's gravitational potentials and quantitative conclusions would be invalid.
tag.evidence_quote: Today's LSBGs have similar dark-matter fractions and angular momenta to high-surface-brightness galaxies (HSBGs; μ < 23 mag arcsec−2), but larger effective radii (×2.5 for UDGs) and lower fractions of dense, star-forming gas (more than ×6 less in UDGs than HSBGs).

y.title: Testing Modified Newtonian Dynamics with Low Surface Brightness Galaxies: Rotation Curve Fits
y.abstract: We present modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) fits to 15 rotation curves of low surface brightness (LSB) galaxies. Good fits are readily found, although for a few galaxies minor adjustments to the inclination are needed. Reasonable values for the stellar mass-to-light ratios are found, as well as an approximately constant value for the total (gas and stars) mass-to-light ratio. We show that the LSB galaxies investigated here lie on the one, unique Tully-Fisher relation, as predicted by MOND. The scatter on the Tully-Fisher relation can be completely explained by the observed scatter in the total mass-to-light ratio. We address the question of whether MOND can fit any arbitrary rotation curve by constructing a plausible fake model galaxy. While MOND is unable to fit this hypothetical galaxy, a normal dark-halo fit is readily found, showing that dark matter fits are much less selective in producing fits. The good fits to rotation curves of LSB galaxies support MOND, especially because these are galaxies with large mass discrepancies deep in the MOND regime.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that MOND successfully fits rotation curves of 15 low surface brightness galaxies, with these galaxies lying on a single Tully-Fisher relation as predicted by MOND, while also demonstrating that MOND is more selective than dark-halo fitting.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim requires Q2 (Newtonian dynamics break down below a0) since the fits are MOND fits using the modified force law. It requires Q1 (baryons alone explain dynamics) since the fits use only gas and stars with no dark matter. It requires Q3 (Tully-Fisher follows from the force law) since the paper explicitly tests this MOND prediction and presents it as supporting evidence.
tag.evidence_quote: We show that the LSB galaxies investigated here lie on the one, unique Tully-Fisher relation, as predicted by MOND. The scatter on the Tully-Fisher relation can be completely explained by the observed scatter in the total mass-to-light ratio.

judge.conjunction: Low-surface-brightness galaxies form through supernova feedback and tidal processes that produce their diffuse, gas-poor profiles [x], and their rotation curves and Tully-Fisher relation are well reproduced by MOND [y].
judge.x_background_statement: LSBGs form and evolve within dark matter halos in a ΛCDM cosmology; dark matter provides the gravitational potential wells in which gas collapses, star formation proceeds, and tidal interactions shape galaxy profiles.
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy dynamics, including LSBG rotation curves and the Tully-Fisher relation, are explained entirely by baryonic matter under MOND, without any dark matter.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P1 asserts that most matter in the universe is non-baryonic dark matter, and x's entire formation scenario is simulated within dark matter halos that provide the gravitational scaffolding for gas collapse and tidal interactions. Q1 asserts that galaxy dynamics are explained by baryons alone with no dark matter. If dark matter halos exist and drive LSBG formation as x claims, MOND's dark-matter-free explanation of LSBG dynamics is either redundant or contradictory; if MOND suffices for dynamics without dark matter, the halo-based formation pathway in x loses its gravitational foundation.
judge.orphan_conclusion: LSBGs require dark matter halos for their formation history but modified gravity (MOND) without dark matter for their present-day rotation curve dynamics.
judge.notes: The conflict is ontological (does dark matter exist?), not a scoping difference. Horizon-AGN is a ΛCDM simulation that explicitly tracks dark matter fractions, and the formation pathway (gas collapse in halos, tidal broadening) depends on the halo potential. Paper y's MOND fits are presented as evidence against dark matter. A verifier should check whether x's formation mechanism could be reformulated without dark-matter-halo dependence (e.g., if feedback and tidal processes could operate in a MOND cosmology), which would weaken x_depends_on_p. Also check whether MOND proponents offer alternative LSBG formation scenarios that would make the orphan conclusion less clearly rejected by Q.

x.title: High-Resolution Rotation Curves of Low Surface Brightness Galaxies. II. Mass Models
x.abstract: We present mass models for a sample of 30 high-resolution rotation curves of low surface brightness galaxies. We fit both pseudoisothermal (core dominated) and cold dark matter (CDM; cusp dominated) halos for a wide variety of assumptions about the stellar mass-to-light ratio. We find that the pseudoisothermal model provides superior fits. CDM fits show systematic deviations from the data and often have a small statistical likelihood of being the appropriate model. The distribution of concentration parameters is too broad, and has too low a mean, to be explained by low-density, flat CDM (ΛCDM). This failing becomes more severe as increasing allowance is made for stellar mass: Navarro, Frenk, & White (NFW) model fits require uncomfortably low mass-to-light ratios. In contrast, the maximum disk procedure does often succeed in predicting the inner shape of the rotation curves, but it requires uncomfortably large stellar mass-to-light ratios. The data do admit reasonable stellar population mass-to-light ratios if halos have cores rather than cusps.

tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis assumes galaxies are surrounded by dark matter halos (P1) and uses Newtonian dynamics to infer mass distributions from rotation curves (P2). If dark matter does not exist or if Newtonian dynamics break down at low accelerations, the mass models and their fitted halo profiles would be meaningless.

y.title: The Published Extended Rotation Curves of Spiral Galaxies: Confrontation with Modified Dynamics
y.abstract: A sample of 22 spiral galaxy rotation curves, measured in the 21 cm line of neutral hydrogen, is considered in the context of Milgrom's modified dynamics (MOND). Combined with the previous, highly selected sample of Begeman et al., this constitutes the current total sample of galaxies with published (or available) extended rotation curves and photometric observations of the light distribution. This is the observational basis of present quantitative understanding of the discrepancy between the visible mass and classical dynamical mass in galaxies. It is found that the gravitational force calculated from the observed distribution of luminous material and gas by use of the simple MOND formula can account for the overall shape and amplitude of these 22 rotation curves, and in some cases, the predicted curve agrees with the observed rotation curve in detail. The fitted rotation curves have, in 13 cases, only one free parameter, which is the mass-to-light ratio of the luminous disk; in nine cases, there is an additional free parameter, which is M / L of a central bulge or light concentration. The values of the global M / L (bulge plus disk) are reasonable and, when the gas mass is also included, show a scatter consistent with that in the Tully-Fisher relation. The success of the MOND prescription in predicting the rotation curves in this larger, less stringently selected sample lends further support to the idea that dynamics or gravity is non-Newtonian in the limit of low acceleration and that it is unnecessary to invoke the presence of large quantities of unseen matter.
