tag.dependence_explanation: The claim requires that galaxy dynamics can be explained by baryonic matter alone (Q1) and that Newtonian dynamics break down at low accelerations, with the MOND formula replacing them (Q2). If dark matter were necessary or Newtonian dynamics held at all accelerations, the claim that MOND accounts for the curves without unseen matter would fail.
tag.evidence_quote: It is found that the gravitational force calculated from the observed distribution of luminous material and gas by use of the simple MOND formula can account for the overall shape and amplitude of these 22 rotation curves... The success of the MOND prescription in predicting the rotation curves in this larger, less stringently selected sample lends further support to the idea that dynamics or gravity is non-Newtonian in the limit of low acceleration and that it is unnecessary to invoke the presence of large quantities of unseen matter.

judge.conjunction: Low-surface-brightness galaxies form through early rapid star formation whose supernova feedback flattens gas-density profiles, followed by tidal perturbations and ram-pressure stripping [x], while the rotation curves of spiral galaxies can be reproduced from the observed baryonic distribution alone using the MOND formula without requiring dark matter [y].
judge.x_background_statement: The formation and evolution of LSBGs is simulated within a Lambda-CDM cosmological framework in which dark matter halos provide the gravitational potential wells within which baryonic processes—star formation, supernova feedback, tidal interactions, and ram-pressure stripping—operate, and LSBGs possess dark-matter fractions comparable to high-surface-brightness galaxies.
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy rotation curves can be fully accounted for by the observed distribution of luminous material and gas via the MOND formula, making it unnecessary to invoke large quantities of unseen (non-baryonic dark) matter.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P1 asserts that most matter in the universe is non-baryonic dark matter that provides the gravitational scaffolding for galaxy formation and evolution, while Q1 asserts that galaxy dynamics are explained by baryonic matter alone with no dark matter required. These are mutually exclusive ontological commitments: either dark matter halos exist and dominate galactic gravitational potentials, or they do not and modified gravity replaces them.
judge.orphan_conclusion: The baryonic formation mechanisms of LSBGs—early rapid star formation, supernova feedback, tidal perturbations, and ram-pressure stripping—proceed in the same manner regardless of whether dark matter halons exist, since galaxy dynamics can be explained without dark matter.
judge.notes: Paper x uses Horizon-AGN, an explicitly Lambda-CDM cosmological hydrodynamical simulation, and directly reports dark-matter fractions for LSBGs, tying the formation pathways to dark matter halos. Paper y explicitly argues dark matter is unnecessary. The orphan conclusion follows because in P's web the formation mechanisms are inseparable from dark matter halos (tidal fields, merger histories, potential wells), while in Q's web without dark matter halos the gravitational potential and thus the formation pathways would differ qualitatively. A human verifier should confirm that no MOND-compatible LSBG formation model reproduces the same feedback-plus-tidal pathway, which would weaken the orphan conclusion. Also verify that Sanders (1996) does not discuss LSBGs specifically, ensuring no direct surface-level contradiction.

x.title: THE DARK MATTER DENSITY PROFILE OF THE FORNAX DWARF
x.abstract: We construct axisymmetric Schwarzschild models to measure the mass profile of the Local Group dwarf galaxy Fornax. These models require no assumptions to be made about the orbital anisotropy of the stars, as is the case for commonly used Jeans models. We test a variety of parameterizations of dark matter density profiles and find cored models with uniform density ρ c = (1.6 ± 0.1) × 10 −2 M ☉ pc −3 fit significantly better than the cuspy halos predicted by cold dark matter simulations. We also construct models with an intermediate-mass black hole, but are unable to make a detection. We place a 1σ upper limit on the mass of a potential intermediate-mass black hole at M • ⩽ 3.2 × 10 4 M ☉ .

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that cored dark matter density profiles fit the Fornax dwarf galaxy significantly better than the cuspy halos predicted by cold dark matter simulations.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis assumes dark matter exists and dominates the mass budget (P1), and uses Schwarzschild models based on Newtonian dynamics to infer the mass profile from stellar motions (P2). If dark matter does not exist or if dynamics deviate from Newtonian at low accelerations, the inferred dark matter density profile would be meaningless.
tag.evidence_quote: We test a variety of parameterizations of dark matter density profiles and find cored models with uniform density ρ c = (1.6 ± 0.1) × 10 −2 M ☉ pc −3 fit significantly better than the cuspy halos predicted by cold dark matter simulations.

y.title: Dynamical friction in modified Newtonian dynamics
y.abstract: We have tested a previous analytical estimate of the dynamical friction time-scale in modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) with fully non-linear N-body simulations. The simulations confirm that the dynamical friction time-scale is significantly shorter in MOND than in equivalent Newtonian systems, i.e. systems with the same phase-space distribution of baryons and additional dark matter. An apparent conflict between this result and the long time-scales determined for bars to slow and mergers to be completed in previous N-body simulations of MOND systems is explained. The confirmation of the short dynamical-friction time-scale in MOND underlines the challenge that the Fornax dwarf spheroidal poses to the viability of MOND.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that dynamical friction timescales are significantly shorter in MOND than in equivalent Newtonian dark-matter systems, posing a challenge to MOND's viability in explaining the Fornax dwarf spheroidal.
tag.dependence_explanation: The short dynamical-friction timescale is a direct consequence of MOND's modified force law at low accelerations (Q2). Without the breakdown of Newtonian dynamics below a0, there is no MOND-specific enhancement of dynamical friction to report.
tag.evidence_quote: The simulations confirm that the dynamical friction time-scale is significantly shorter in MOND than in equivalent Newtonian systems, i.e. systems with the same phase-space distribution of baryons and additional dark matter.

judge.conjunction: Studies of the Fornax dwarf spheroidal reveal that cored dark matter density profiles fit significantly better than the cuspy halos predicted by cold dark matter simulations [x], while dynamical friction timescales in MOND are significantly shorter than in equivalent Newtonian dark-matter systems, posing a challenge to MOND's viability for this same galaxy [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Newtonian dynamics hold at the very low accelerations prevailing in dwarf spheroidals, so that stellar orbits in the Schwarzschild models reliably trace the gravitational potential and thereby constrain the dark matter density profile.
judge.y_background_statement: Newtonian dynamics break down below the characteristic acceleration a0, so that the MOND force law governs dynamical friction in the Fornax dwarf and produces shorter timescales than in equivalent Newtonian systems.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P2 asserts Newtonian dynamics remain valid at low accelerations such as those in dwarf spheroidals; Q2 asserts they break down below a0. Both claims concern the same low-acceleration regime of the same galaxy, so the two background statements cannot simultaneously hold.
judge.orphan_conclusion: The Fornax dwarf spheroidal cannot be explained by either the dark matter paradigm or by modified gravity, requiring a fundamentally new theoretical framework.
judge.notes: Both papers study the same object (Fornax dwarf spheroidal) in the same low-acceleration regime, so no regime separation rescues the conjunction. Paper x's Schwarzschild models assume Newtonian gravity to infer the DM density profile; if MOND's modified force law applies, the inferred mass distribution changes fundamentally. Paper y's short dynamical-friction timescale is a direct consequence of the MOND force law at low accelerations. A human verifier should confirm that the Schwarzschild method in paper x genuinely relies on Newtonian dynamics at the relevant acceleration scales (it does, since the method solves the collisionless Boltzmann equation in a Newtonian potential). The orphan conclusion—ruling out both paradigms—is rejected by both communities: CDM proponents invoke baryonic feedback to create cores, and MOND proponents argue the friction issue may be mitigated by additional physics.

x.title: Simulations of Galaxy Formation in a Λ Cold Dark Matter Universe. II. The Fine Structure of Simulated Galactic Disks
x.abstract: We present a detailed analysis of the disk component of a simulated galaxy formed in the ΛCDM cosmogony. At redshift z = 0, two distinct dynamical components are easily identified solely on the basis of the orbital parameters of stars in the galaxy: a slowly rotating, centrally concentrated spheroid and a disklike component largely supported by rotation. The disk may be further decomposed into a thin, dynamically cold component with stars on nearly circular orbits and a hotter, thicker component with orbital parameters transitional between the thin disk and the spheroid. Supporting evidence for the presence of distinct thick- and thin-disk components is provided, as in the Milky Way, by the double-exponential vertical structure of the disk and in abrupt changes in the vertical velocity distribution as a function of stellar age. The dynamical origin of these components offers intriguing clues to the assembly of spheroids and disks in the Milky Way and other spiral galaxies. The spheroid is old and has essentially no stars younger than the time elapsed since the last major accretion event, ~8 Gyr ago for the system we consider here. The majority of thin-disk stars, on the other hand, form after the merging activity is over, although a significant fraction (~15%) of thin-disk stars are old enough to predate the last major merger event. This unexpected population of old-disk stars consists mainly of the tidal debris of satellites whose orbital plane was coincident with the disk and whose orbits were circularized by dynamical friction prior to full disruption. More than half of the stars in the thick disk share this origin, part of a trend that becomes more pronounced with age: 9 out of 10 stars presently in the old (age of ≳10 Gyr) disk component were actually brought into the disk by satellites. By contrast, only one in two stars belonging to the old spheroid are tidal debris; the rest may be traced to a major merger event that dispersed the luminous progenitor at z ~ 1.5 and seeded the formation of the spheroid. Our results highlight the role of satellite accretion events in shaping the disk, as well as the spheroidal, component and reveal some of the clues to the assembly process of a galaxy preserved in the detailed dynamics of old stellar populations.

tag.main_claim: Abadi et al. show that in ΛCDM simulations, satellite accretion events shape the thin and thick disk components of galaxies, with most old disk stars being tidal debris from accreted satellites.
tag.dependence_explanation: The simulation is performed within the ΛCDM cosmogony, which requires non-baryonic dark matter (P1) to form halos and drive hierarchical merging, and uses Newtonian dynamics (P2) to compute satellite orbits, dynamical friction, and tidal disruption. If dark matter does not exist or if dynamics is modified at low accelerations, the merger histories and dynamical friction effects that produce the disk components would differ fundamentally.
tag.evidence_quote: We present a detailed analysis of the disk component of a simulated galaxy formed in the ΛCDM cosmogony.

y.title: Numerical Solutions of the External Field Effect on the Radial Acceleration in Disk Galaxies
y.abstract: Abstract In modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND)-based theories, the strong equivalence principle is generically broken in an idiosyncratic manner, manifested in the action of an “external field effect” (EFE). The internal dynamics in a self-gravitating system is affected even by a constant external field. In disk galaxies, the EFE can induce warps and modify the rotational speeds. Due to the nonlinearity of MOND, it is difficult to derive analytic expressions of this important effect in a disk. Here we study numerically the EFE in two nonrelativistic Lagrangian theories of MOND: the “Aquadratic–Lagrangian” theory (AQUAL) and “Quasilinear MOND” (QUMOND). For AQUAL, we consider only the axisymmetric field configurations with the external field along the disk axis, or a spherical galaxy with test-particle orbits inclined to the external field. For the more manageable QUMOND, we also calculate the three-dimensional field configurations, with the external field inclined to the disk axis. We investigate in particular to what degree an external field modifies the quasi-flat part of rotation curves. While our QUMOND results agree well with published numerical results in QUMOND, we find that AQUAL predicts weaker EFE than published AQUAL results. However, AQUAL still predicts stronger EFE than QUMOND, which demonstrates current theoretical uncertainties. We also illustrate how the MOND prediction on the rising part of the rotation curve, in the inner parts, depends largely on disk thickness but only weakly on a plausible external field for a fixed galaxy model. Finally, we summarize our results for the outer parts as an improved, approximate analytic expression.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that in MOND theories, AQUAL predicts a weaker external field effect than previously published AQUAL results but a stronger EFE than QUMOND, demonstrating theoretical uncertainties in MOND predictions for disk galaxy rotation curves.
tag.dependence_explanation: The external field effect is a unique consequence of MOND's violation of the strong equivalence principle, which arises only because Newtonian dynamics break down at low accelerations (Q2). The entire analysis assumes galaxy dynamics are governed by baryonic matter alone without dark matter (Q1); if dark matter were present, there would be no EFE to compute.
tag.evidence_quote: In modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND)-based theories, the strong equivalence principle is generically broken in an idiosyncratic manner, manifested in the action of an "external field effect" (EFE). The internal dynamics in a self-gravitating system is affected even by a constant external field.

judge.conjunction: Studies of galactic disk dynamics show that satellite accretion events shape the thin and thick disk components of galaxies [x], while the external field effect modifies rotational speeds in disk galaxies [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Most matter in the universe is non-baryonic dark matter, forming halos and subhalos whose dynamical friction drives satellite accretion and shapes galactic disk components.
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy dynamics are explained by baryonic matter alone, without dark matter, and the external field effect arises from the nonlinearity of MOND's modified force law.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P1 asserts that non-baryonic dark matter dominates the universe's mass budget and drives galaxy formation, while Q1 asserts that galaxy dynamics require no dark matter at all. These are mutually exclusive: either dark matter exists and dominates, or it does not.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Galactic disk structure is shaped by both dark-matter-driven satellite accretion events and by the MOND external field effect on rotation curves, combining formation history and modified gravity.
judge.notes: Paper x's ΛCDM simulation relies on dark matter subhalos for dynamical friction that circularizes satellite orbits into the disk; without dark matter (as in MOND) this mechanism would not operate as simulated. Paper y's EFE is a MOND-specific prediction with no counterpart in ΛCDM. A reviewer combining both claims would implicitly assume both that dark matter exists and that it does not. The conflict is between fundamental frameworks, not between physical regimes that could be separately scoped.

x.title: The core–cusp problem: a matter of perspective
x.abstract: The existence of two kinematically and chemically distinct stellar subpopulations in the Sculptor and Fornax dwarf galaxies offers the opportunity to constrain the density profile of their matter haloes by measuring the mass contained within the well-separated half-light radii of the two metallicity subpopulations. Walker and Peñarrubia have used this approach to argue that data for these galaxies are consistent with constant-density ‘cores’ in their inner regions and rule out ‘cuspy’ Navarro–Frenk–White (NFW) profiles with high statistical significance, particularly in the case of Sculptor. We test the validity of these claims using dwarf galaxies in the APOSTLE (A Project Of Simulating The Local Environment) Λ cold dark matter cosmological hydrodynamic simulations of analogues of the Local Group. These galaxies all have NFW dark matter density profiles and a subset of them develop two distinct metallicity subpopulations reminiscent of Sculptor and Fornax. We apply a method analogous to that of Walker and Peñarrubia to a sample of 50 simulated dwarfs and find that this procedure often leads to a statistically significant detection of a core in the profile when in reality there is a cusp. Although multiple factors contribute to these failures, the main cause is a violation of the assumption of spherical symmetry upon which the mass estimators are based. The stellar populations of the simulated dwarfs tend to be significantly elongated and, in several cases, the two metallicity populations have different asphericity and are misaligned. As a result, a wide range of slopes of the density profile are inferred depending on the angle from which the galaxy is viewed.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that the Walker–Peñarrubia method for inferring dwarf galaxy halo density profiles can falsely detect cores in cuspy NFW dark matter haloes, primarily because the assumed spherical symmetry is violated by elongated and misaligned stellar populations.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis presupposes that dwarf galaxies reside in non-baryonic dark matter haloes with NFW density profiles, as generated in ΛCDM cosmological simulations; rejecting P1 would remove the premise that such haloes exist and that the core–cusp problem is meaningful.
tag.evidence_quote: These galaxies all have NFW dark matter density profiles and a subset of them develop two distinct metallicity subpopulations reminiscent of Sculptor and Fornax. We apply a method analogous to that of Walker and Peñarrubia to a sample of 50 simulated dwarfs and find that this procedure often leads to a statistically significant detection of a core in the profile when in reality there is a cusp.

y.title: Testing the Strong Equivalence Principle. II. Relating the External Field Effect in Galaxy Rotation Curves to the Large-scale Structure of the Universe
y.abstract: Abstract Theories of modified gravity generically violate the strong equivalence principle, so that the internal dynamics of a self-gravitating system in freefall depends on the strength of the external gravitational field (the external field effect). We fit rotation curves (RCs) from the SPARC database with a model inspired by Milgromian dynamics (MOND), which relates the outer shape of an RC to the external Newtonian field from the large-scale baryonic matter distribution through a dimensionless parameter e N. We obtain a > 4σ statistical detection of the external field effect (i.e. e N > 0 on average), confirming previous results. We then locate the SPARC galaxies in the cosmic web of the nearby universe and find a striking contrast in the fitted e N values for galaxies in underdense versus overdense regions. Galaxies in an underdense region between 22 and 45 Mpc from the celestial axis in the northern sky have RC fits consistent with e N ≃ 0, while those in overdense regions adjacent to the CfA2 Great Wall and the Perseus−Pisces Supercluster return e N that are a factor of two larger than the median for SPARC galaxies. We also calculate independent estimates of e N from galaxy survey data and find that they agree with the e N inferred from the RCs within the uncertainties, the chief uncertainty being the spatial distribution of baryons not contained in galaxies or clusters.

tag.main_claim: Chae et al. detect the external field effect in galaxy rotation curves at >4σ significance, showing that internal galactic dynamics depend on the external gravitational field from large-scale baryonic matter, consistent with MOND.
tag.dependence_explanation: The external field effect exists only when Newtonian dynamics break down below a0 (Q2), making internal dynamics of a self-gravitating system depend on the external field strength. The model also assumes the external field is sourced by baryonic matter alone (Q1); if dark matter dominated the gravitational field (P1), the baryonic-based external field estimates would be invalid and the EFE would not arise.
tag.evidence_quote: Theories of modified gravity generically violate the strong equivalence principle, so that the internal dynamics of a self-gravitating system in freefall depends on the strength of the external gravitational field (the external field effect). We fit rotation curves (RCs) from the SPARC database with a model inspired by Milgromian dynamics (MOND), which relates the outer shape of an RC to the external Newtonian field from the large-scale baryonic matter distribution through a dimensionless parameter e N.

judge.conjunction: Recent studies have shown that the Walker–Peñarrubia method can falsely detect cores in cuspy NFW dark matter haloes of dwarf galaxies due to asphericity [x], and that the external field effect in galaxy rotation curves is detected at >4σ significance, consistent with MOND [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Dwarf galaxies are embedded in cuspy NFW dark matter haloes composed of non-baryonic dark matter, whose density profiles can be studied via stellar kinematics.
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy rotation curves are governed by baryonic matter alone through MOND's modified force law, which predicts the external field effect without dark matter.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: Paper x's claim that NFW dark matter haloes exist and have cuspy profiles requires that non-baryonic dark matter dominates galaxy dynamics (P1). Paper y's claim that the external field effect is detected and is consistent with MOND requires that galaxy dynamics are explained by baryonic matter alone without dark matter (Q1). If dark matter haloes exist, MOND's force law is not the explanation for galaxy dynamics and the EFE should not appear; if MOND governs dynamics without dark matter, there are no NFW haloes in which cores could be falsely detected.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Galaxy dynamics are governed by both collisionless dark matter haloes with NFW density profiles (whose cusps may be misidentified as cores) and by modified gravity acting on baryonic matter alone (producing the external field effect).
judge.notes: Paper x works entirely within ΛCDM simulations (APOSTLE), explicitly assuming NFW dark matter haloes exist. Paper y explicitly frames the EFE detection as consistent with MOND, which requires no dark matter. A literature review citing both side-by-side as 'recent results in galaxy dynamics' would implicitly endorse a hybrid picture that neither ΛCDM nor MOND accepts. The conflict is fundamental (dark matter exists vs. it does not) and cannot be resolved by restricting to different galaxy types or regimes, since both frameworks claim to explain all galaxy dynamics.

x.title: The Structure of Cold Dark Matter Halos
x.abstract: We use N-body simulations to investigate the structure of dark halos in the standard cold dark matter cosmogony. Halos are excised from simulations of cosmologically representative regions and are resimulated individually at high resolution. We study objects with masses ranging from those of dwarf galaxy halos to those of rich galaxy clusters. The spherically averaged density profiles of all our halos can be fitted over two decades in radius by scaling a simple "universal" profile. The characteristic over- density of a halo, or equivalently its concentration, correlates strongly with halo mass in a way that reflects the mass dependence of the epoch of halo formation. Halo profiles are approximately isothermal over a large range in radii but are significantly shallower than r -2 near the center and steeper than r-2 near the virial radius. Matching the observed rotation curves of disk galaxies requires disk mass-to-light ratios to increase systematically with luminosity. Further, it suggests that the halos of bright galaxies depend only weakly on galaxy luminosity and have circular velocities significantly lower than the disk rotation speed. This may explain why luminosity and dynamics are uncorrelated in observed samples of binary galaxies and of satellite/spiral systems. For galaxy clusters, our halo models are consistent both with the presence of giant arcs and with the observed structure of the intracluster medium, and they suggest a simple explanation for the disparate estimates of cluster core radii found by previous authors. Our results also highlight two shortcomings of the CDM model. CDM halos are too concentrated to be consistent with the halo parameters inferred for dwarf irregulars, and the predicted abundance of galaxy halos is larger than the observed abundance of galaxies. The first problem may imply that the core structure of dwarf galaxies was altered by the galaxy formation process, and the second problem may imply that galaxies failed to form (or remain undetected) in many dark halos.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that cold dark matter halos in cosmological N-body simulations follow a universal density profile with mass-dependent concentration, and that this profile's implications for galaxy rotation curves and galaxy clusters are broadly consistent with observations, though CDM halos are too concentrated for dwarf irregulars.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire simulation framework assumes dark matter halos exist and dominate structure formation (P1), uses Newtonian gravity in N-body simulations (P2), and models galaxy clusters as dark-matter-dominated systems when comparing to lensing and intracluster medium observations (P4).
tag.evidence_quote: We use N-body simulations to investigate the structure of dark halos in the standard cold dark matter cosmogony. Halos are excised from simulations of cosmologically representative regions and are resimulated individually at high resolution.

y.title: Galaxy clusters in Milgromian dynamics: Missing matter, hydrostatic bias, and the external field effect
y.abstract: We study the mass distribution of galaxy clusters in Milgromian dynamics, or modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND). We focus on five galaxy clusters from the X-COP sample, for which high-quality data are available on both the baryonic mass distribution (gas and stars) and internal dynamics (from the hydrostatic equilibrium of hot gas and the Sunyaev–Zeldovich effect). We confirm that galaxy clusters require additional ‘missing matter’ in MOND, although the required amount is drastically reduced with respect to the non-baryonic dark matter in the context of Newtonian dynamics. We studied the spatial distribution of the missing matter by fitting the acceleration profiles of the clusters with a Bayesian method, finding that a physical density profile with an inner core and an outer r −4 decline (giving a finite total mass) provide good fits within ∼1 Mpc. At larger radii, the fit results are less satisfactory but the combination of the MOND external field effect and hydrostatic bias (quantified as 10%–40%) can play a key role. The missing mass must be more centrally concentrated than the intracluster medium (ICM). For relaxed clusters (A1795, A2029, A2142), the ratio of missing-to-visible mass is around 1 − 5 at R ≃ 200 − 300 kpc and decreases to 0.4 − 1.1 at R ≃ 2 − 3 Mpc, showing that the total amount of missing mass is smaller than or comparable to the ICM mass. For clusters with known merger signatures (A644 and A2319), this global ratio increases up to ∼5 but may indicate out-of-equilibrium dynamics rather than actual missing mass. We discuss various possibilities regarding the nature of the extra mass, in particular ‘missing baryons’ in the form of pressure-confined cold gas clouds with masses of < 10 5 M ⊙ and sizes of < 50 pc.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that in MOND, galaxy clusters require additional 'missing matter' with a cored density profile declining as r^-4, but the amount is drastically reduced compared to Newtonian dark matter, and the missing mass is more centrally concentrated than the intracluster medium.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis uses MOND's modified force law (Q2) to compute acceleration profiles from baryonic mass, and interprets the residual mass discrepancy as modified gravity plus possible missing baryons rather than collisionless dark matter (Q4), directly contrasting with the dark matter interpretation.
tag.evidence_quote: We confirm that galaxy clusters require additional 'missing matter' in MOND, although the required amount is drastically reduced with respect to the non-baryonic dark matter in the context of Newtonian dynamics.

judge.conjunction: N-body simulations show that cold dark matter halos follow a universal density profile broadly consistent with galaxy cluster observations [x], while MOND analyses find that galaxy clusters require significantly less missing matter than Newtonian predictions, concentrated in a cored r^{-4} profile [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Newtonian dynamics and general relativity hold at all accelerations, including the very low accelerations characteristic of galactic and cluster halos, so that N-body simulations computed with Newtonian gravity faithfully describe real halo structure.
judge.y_background_statement: Newtonian dynamics break down below the characteristic acceleration a0, so that galaxy cluster dynamics must be computed using the MOND force law rather than Newtonian gravity.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P2 asserts Newtonian dynamics hold at very low accelerations; Q2 asserts they break down below a0. Paper x's N-body simulation results are valid only if Newtonian gravity applies throughout the halo, while paper y's MOND analysis is valid only if Newtonian gravity fails in the same regime. Both cannot be true.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Galaxy cluster mass profiles are explained partly by collisionless dark matter halos following the universal NFW profile and partly by modified-gravity effects that reduce the required dark matter, combining both frameworks' successes into a hybrid picture.
judge.notes: Both papers study galaxy clusters at overlapping physical scales (~100 kpc to several Mpc), so no regime separation resolves the conflict. Paper x's CDM simulation assumes Newtonian gravity at all accelerations (P2); paper y's MOND analysis assumes Newtonian breakdown below a0 (Q2). The orphan conclusion—a hybrid dark-matter-plus-modified-gravity model— is rejected by both frameworks: P holds that all cluster mass discrepancy is collisionless dark matter with no modified gravity, and Q holds that there is no collisionless dark matter and the discrepancy arises from modified gravity (plus possibly missing baryons). A literature-review writer citing both without flagging the dynamical incompatibility implicitly endorses this orphan hybrid.

x.title: ΛCDM is Consistent with SPARC Radial Acceleration Relation
x.abstract: Abstract Recent analysis of the Spitzer Photometry and Accurate Rotation Curve (SPARC) galaxy sample found a surprisingly tight relation between the radial acceleration inferred from the rotation curves and the acceleration due to the baryonic components of the disk. It has been suggested that this relation may be evidence for new physics, beyond ΛCDM. In this Letter, we show that 32 galaxies from the MUGS2 match the SPARC acceleration relation. These cosmological simulations of star-forming, rotationally supported disks were simulated with a WMAP3 ΛCDM cosmology, and match the SPARC acceleration relation with less scatter than the observational data. These results show that this acceleration relation is a consequence of dissipative collapse of baryons, rather than being evidence for exotic dark-sector physics or new dynamical laws.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that the SPARC radial acceleration relation arises naturally from dissipative collapse of baryons in ΛCDM simulations, rather than requiring modified dynamics or new fundamental laws.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim relies on P1 because the simulations are ΛCDM cosmological simulations with dark matter halos; without dark matter the simulation setup is invalid. It relies on P2 because the simulations use Newtonian gravity, so if dynamics break down at low accelerations the simulated relation would be meaningless. It directly asserts P3, that the radial acceleration relation emerges from galaxy formation physics rather than being a fundamental law.
tag.evidence_quote: These cosmological simulations of star-forming, rotationally supported disks were simulated with a WMAP3 ΛCDM cosmology, and match the SPARC acceleration relation with less scatter than the observational data. These results show that this acceleration relation is a consequence of dissipative collapse of baryons, rather than being evidence for exotic dark-sector physics or new dynamical laws.

y.title: On the fundamentality of the radial acceleration relation for late-type galaxy dynamics
y.abstract: ABSTRACT Galaxies have been observed to exhibit a level of simplicity unexpected in the complex galaxy formation scenario posited by standard cosmology. This is particularly apparent in their dynamics, where scaling relations display much regularity and little intrinsic scatter. However, the parameters responsible for this simplicity have not been identified. Using the Spitzer Photometry & Accurate Rotation Curves galaxy catalogue, we argue that the radial acceleration relation (RAR) between galaxies’ baryonic and total dynamical accelerations is the fundamental 1D correlation governing the radial (in-disc) dynamics of late-type galaxies. In particular, we show that the RAR cannot be tightened by the inclusion of any other available galaxy property, that it is the strongest projection of galaxies’ radial dynamical parameter space, and that all other statistical radial dynamical correlations stem from the RAR plus the non-dynamical correlations present in our sample. We further provide evidence that the RAR’s fundamentality is unique in that the second most significant dynamical relation does not possess any of these features. Our analysis reveals the root cause of the correlations present in galaxies’ radial dynamics: they are nothing but facets of the RAR. These results have important ramifications for galaxy formation theory because they imply that to explain statistically late-type galaxy dynamics within the disc it is necessary and sufficient to explain the RAR and lack of any significant, partially independent correlation. While simple in some modified dynamics models, this poses a challenge to standard cosmology.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that the radial acceleration relation is the fundamental correlation governing late-type galaxy radial dynamics, such that explaining it is necessary and sufficient to account for their in-disc dynamics.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's claim that the RAR is fundamental—rather than an emergent product of galaxy formation and feedback—directly depends on Q3, which asserts that galaxy scaling relations follow from the force law itself. If Q3 were rejected and the RAR instead emerged from baryonic physics (as P3 holds), the claim of fundamentality would be undercut.
tag.evidence_quote: While simple in some modified dynamics models, this poses a challenge to standard cosmology.

judge.conjunction: Studies have shown that the radial acceleration relation arises from dissipative baryonic collapse in ΛCDM simulations [x], while the RAR serves as the fundamental correlation governing late-type galaxy dynamics [y].
judge.x_background_statement: The radial acceleration relation is a consequence of dissipative collapse of baryons during galaxy formation, not a fundamental dynamical law.
judge.y_background_statement: The radial acceleration relation is the fundamental, irreducible correlation governing galaxy radial dynamics, serving as the root cause from which all other radial dynamical correlations stem.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: If the RAR is truly fundamental (irreducible, the root cause of all dynamical correlations), it cannot simultaneously be a mere emergent consequence of dissipative baryonic collapse during galaxy formation. A relation cannot be both ontologically fundamental and emergent from complex astrophysical processes.
judge.orphan_conclusion: ΛCDM galaxy formation processes naturally produce the fundamental dynamical law governing galaxy rotation.
judge.notes: Paper x explicitly states the RAR is 'a consequence of dissipative collapse of baryons, rather than being evidence for…new dynamical laws,' directly invoking P3. Paper y explicitly states the RAR is 'the fundamental 1D correlation' and that its fundamentality is 'simple in some modified dynamics models' while it 'poses a challenge to standard cosmology,' aligning with Q3. The orphan conclusion—that galaxy formation produces a fundamental law—is rejected by P (the RAR is not a fundamental law) and by Q (the RAR is fundamental but comes from the force law, not from galaxy formation). A human verifier should confirm that paper y's use of 'fundamental' is ontological (about the underlying physics) rather than purely statistical (about correlation strength), since the latter would weaken the dependence on Q3.

x.title: The surprising accuracy of isothermal Jeans modelling of self-interacting dark matter density profiles
x.abstract: ABSTRACT Recent claims of observational evidence for self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) have relied on a semi-analytic method for predicting the density profiles of galaxies and galaxy clusters containing SIDM. We present a thorough description of this method, known as isothermal Jeans modelling, and then test it with a large ensemble of haloes taken from cosmological simulations. Our simulations were run with cold and collisionless dark matter (CDM) as well as two different SIDM models, all with dark matter only variants as well as versions including baryons and relevant galaxy formation physics. Using a mix of different box sizes and resolutions, we study haloes with masses ranging from 3 × 1010 to $3 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{\, M_\odot }$. Overall, we find that the isothermal Jeans model provides as accurate a description of simulated SIDM density profiles as the Navarro–Frenk–White profile does of CDM haloes. We can use the model predictions, compared with the simulated density profiles, to determine the input DM–DM scattering cross-sections used to run the simulations. This works especially well for large cross-sections, while with CDM our results tend to favour non-zero (albeit fairly small) cross-sections, driven by a bias against small cross-sections inherent to our adopted method of sampling the model parameter space. The model works across the whole halo mass range we study, although including baryons leads to DM profiles of intermediate-mass ($10^{12} - 10^{13} \mathrm{\, M_\odot }$) haloes that do not depend strongly on the SIDM cross-section. The tightest constraints will therefore come from lower and higher mass haloes: dwarf galaxies and galaxy clusters.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that isothermal Jeans modelling accurately predicts self-interacting dark matter density profiles across halo masses from dwarf galaxies to galaxy clusters, comparable to how NFW profiles describe CDM haloes.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis presupposes that dark matter exists and dominates galaxy haloes (P1), as it studies both CDM and SIDM haloes. The extension to cluster-scale masses (up to 10^15 M_sun) requires that galaxy clusters are dark-matter-dominated systems (P4).
tag.evidence_quote: Our simulations were run with cold and collisionless dark matter (CDM) as well as two different SIDM models, all with dark matter only variants as well as versions including baryons and relevant galaxy formation physics. Using a mix of different box sizes and resolutions, we study haloes with masses ranging from 3 × 10^10 to 3 × 10^15 M_⊙.

y.title: LoCuSS: Subaru Weak Lensing Study of 30 Galaxy Clusters
y.abstract: We use high-quality Subaru/Suprime-Cam imaging data to conduct a detailed weak lensing study of the distribution of dark matter in a sample of 30 X-ray luminous galaxy clusters at 0.15 $\le z \le$ 0.3. A weak lensing signal is detected at high statistical significance in each cluster, the total signal-to-noise ratio of the detections ranging from 5 to 13. Comparing spherical models to the tangential distortion profiles of the clusters individually, we are unable to discriminate statistically between a singular isothermal sphere (SIS) and Navarro, Frenk, and White (NFW) models. However, when the tangential distortion profiles are combined and then models are fitted to the stacked profile, the SIS model is rejected at 6$\ \sigma$ and 11$\ \sigma$, respectively, for low ($M_{\rm vir}\lt$ 6 $\times$ 10$^{14}\ h^{-1}\ M_\odot$) and high ($M_{\rm vir} \gt $ 6 $\times$ 10$^{14}\ h^{-1}\ M_\odot$) mass bins. We also used individual cluster NFW model fits to investigate the relationship between the cluster mass and the concentration, finding that the concentration ($c_{\rm vir}$) decreases with increasing cluster mass ($M_{\rm vir}$). The best-fit $c_{\rm vir}$–$M_{\rm vir}$ relation is: $c_{\rm vir}$($M_{\rm vir}$) $=$ 8.75$^{+4.13}_{-2.89} \times$ ($M_{\rm vir}/$10$^{14}\ h^{-1}\ M_\odot$)$^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha \approx$ 0.40$\ \pm\ $0.19: i.e., a non-zero slope is detected at 2$\ \sigma$ significance. This relation gives a concentration of $c_{\rm vir} =$ 3.48$^{+1.65}_{-1.15}$ for clusters with $M_{\rm vir} =$ 10$^{15}\ h^{-1}M_\odot$, which is inconsistent at 4$\ \sigma$ significance with the values of $c_{\rm vir} \sim$ 10 reported for strong-lensing-selected clusters. We have found that the measurement error on the cluster mass is smaller at higher over-densities, $\Delta \simeq$ 500–2000, than at the virial over-density, $\Delta_{\rm vir} \simeq$ 110; typical fractional errors at $\Delta \simeq$ 500–2000 are improved to $\ \sigma$($M_\Delta$)$/M_{\Delta } \simeq$ 0.1–0.2 compared with 0.2–0.3 at $\Delta_{\rm vir}$. Furthermore, comparing the 3D spherical mass with the 2D cylinder mass, obtained from the aperture mass method at a given aperture radius, $\theta_\Delta$, reveals $M_{\rm 2D}$($\lt \theta_{\Delta}$)$/M_{\rm 3D}$($\lt r_\Delta = D_{\rm l}\theta_{\Delta}$) $\simeq$ 1.46 and 1.32 for $\Delta =$ 500 and $\Delta_{\rm vir}$, respectively. The amplitude of this offset agrees well with that predicted by integrating an NFW model of cluster-scale halos along the line-of-sight.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that the dark matter distribution in galaxy clusters is better described by NFW profiles than by singular isothermal sphere profiles, and that dark matter halo concentration decreases with increasing cluster mass.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper directly assumes galaxy clusters are dominated by collisionless dark matter (P4, P1) and interprets weak gravitational lensing signals—dependent on GR holding at cluster scales (P2)—as mapping that dark matter distribution, fitting NFW halo profiles derived from CDM simulations.
tag.evidence_quote: We use high-quality Subaru/Suprime-Cam imaging data to conduct a detailed weak lensing study of the distribution of dark matter in a sample of 30 X-ray luminous galaxy clusters at 0.15 ≤ z ≤ 0.3.

judge.conjunction: Recent work has demonstrated both that isothermal Jeans modelling accurately predicts self-interacting dark matter density profiles across halo masses ranging from dwarf galaxies to galaxy clusters [x], and that the dark matter distribution in galaxy clusters is better described by NFW profiles than by singular isothermal sphere profiles, with halo concentration decreasing as cluster mass increases [y].
judge.notes: The two uses of 'isothermal' refer to different concepts: paper x's 'isothermal Jeans modelling' is a semi-analytic method for predicting SIDM density profiles (where 'isothermal' refers to the assumption of thermalization in halo cores), while paper y's 'singular isothermal sphere' is a specific density profile (ρ ∝ r⁻²) that is statistically rejected in favour of NFW—so a reader might conflate the two. More substantively, paper x validates the method partly for SIDM (a dark-matter variant whose large-cross-section models can produce isothermal-like, cored inner profiles), while paper y rejects the singular isothermal sphere profile for cluster dark matter; although SIDM cores are not singular and the two papers address different questions (modelling accuracy vs. profile fitting), a careful reader could perceive tension between the claim that isothermal-type profiles are well supported and the claim that isothermal sphere profiles are disfavoured in clusters. Additionally, paper x notes that with CDM the method carries a bias favouring non-zero cross-sections, and paper x's validation spans SIDM and CDM whereas paper y's results are strictly within standard collisionless CDM.

x.title: DARK MATTER HEATING AND EARLY CORE FORMATION IN DWARF GALAXIES
x.abstract: We present more results from a fully cosmological ΛCDM simulation of a group of isolated dwarf galaxies that has been shown to reproduce the observed stellar mass and cold gas content, resolved star formation histories, and metallicities of dwarfs in the Local Volume. Here we investigate the energetics and timetable of the cusp–core transformation. As suggested by previous work, supernova-driven gas outflows remove dark matter (DM) cusps and create kiloparsec-size cores in all systems having a stellar mass M * > 10 6 M ☉ . The "DM core mass removal efficiency"—dark mass ejected per unit stellar mass—ranges today from a few to a dozen, and increases with decreasing host mass. Because dwarfs form the bulk of their stars prior to redshift 1 and the amount of work required for DM heating and core formation scales approximately as , the unbinding of the DM cusp starts early and the formation of cored profiles is not as energetically onerous as previously claimed. DM particles in the cusp typically migrate to 2–3 core radii after absorbing a few percent of the energy released by supernovae. The present-day slopes of the inner DM mass profiles, Γ ≡ d log M / d log R ≃ 2.5–3, of the simulated "Bashful" and "Doc" dwarfs are similar to those measured in the luminous Fornax and Sculptor dwarf spheroidals. None of the simulated galaxies has a circular velocity profile exceeding 20 km s −1 in the inner 1 kpc, implying that supernova feedback is key to solve the "too-big-to-fail" problem for Milky Way subhalos.

tag.main_claim: Governato et al. show that supernova-driven gas outflows can remove dark matter cusps and create kiloparsec-size cores in dwarf galaxies within ΛCDM, solving the cusp-core and too-big-to-fail problems without modifying gravity.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire mechanism presupposes that non-baryonic dark matter exists and forms cuspy halos (P1), and that standard Newtonian/GR dynamics govern the gravitational potential so that energy injection from supernovae can heat and redistribute DM particles (P2). Without dark matter, there are no cusps to remove; without standard dynamics, the simulated potential wells and feedback energetics would not apply.
tag.evidence_quote: We present more results from a fully cosmological ΛCDM simulation of a group of isolated dwarf galaxies... As suggested by previous work, supernova-driven gas outflows remove dark matter (DM) cusps and create kiloparsec-size cores in all systems having a stellar mass M * > 10 6 M ☉ .

y.title: Forged in fire: cusps, cores and baryons in low-mass dwarf galaxies
y.abstract: We present multiple ultrahigh resolution cosmological hydrodynamic simulations of M⋆ ≃ 104–6.3 Mȯ dwarf galaxies that form within two Mvir = 109.5–10 Mȯ dark matter halo initial conditions. Our simulations rely on the Feedback in Realistic Environments (fire) implementation of star formation feedback and were run with high enough force and mass resolution to directly resolve structure on the ∼200 pc scales. The resultant galaxies sit on the M⋆ versus Mvir relation required to match the Local Group stellar mass function via abundance matching. They have bursty star formation histories and also form with half-light radii and metallicities that broadly match those observed for local dwarfs at the same stellar mass. We demonstrate that it is possible to create a large (∼1 kpc) constant-density dark matter core in a cosmological simulation of an M⋆ ≃ 106.3 Mȯ dwarf galaxy within a typical Mvir = 1010 Mȯ halo – precisely the scale of interest for resolving the ‘too big to fail’ problem. However, these large cores are not ubiquitous and appear to correlate closely with the star formation histories of the dwarfs: dark matter cores are largest in systems that form their stars late (z ≲ 2), after the early epoch of cusp building mergers has ended. Our M⋆ ≃ 104 Mȯ dwarf retains a cuspy dark matter halo density profile that matches that of a dark-matter-only run of the same system. Though ancient, most of the stars in our ultrafaint form after reionization; the ultraviolet field acts mainly to suppress fresh gas accretion, not to boil away gas that is already present in the protodwarf.

tag.main_claim: Onorbe et al. show that baryonic feedback in cosmological hydrodynamic simulations can create large (~1 kpc) dark matter cores in low-mass dwarf galaxies, with core size correlating with star formation history, addressing the 'too big to fail' problem within Lambda-CDM.
tag.dependence_explanation: The simulations are built entirely within the dark matter framework: they assume dwarf galaxies form within dark matter halos (P1) and use standard Newtonian gravity (P2) to model the dynamics. The central claim that feedback redistributes dark matter to create cores requires dark matter to be real and standard dynamics to govern the simulation.
tag.evidence_quote: We present multiple ultrahigh resolution cosmological hydrodynamic simulations of M⋆ ≃ 104–6.3 Mȯ dwarf galaxies that form within two Mvir = 109.5–10 Mȯ dark matter halo initial conditions.

judge.conjunction: Both Governato et al. [x] and Onorbe et al. [y] demonstrate that supernova-driven baryonic feedback in cosmological ΛCDM simulations can transform dark matter cusps into kiloparsec-scale cores in dwarf galaxies, thereby addressing the cusp-core and too-big-to-fail problems without invoking modified gravity.
judge.notes: The conjunction is largely unproblematic since both papers share the ΛCDM framework and reach compatible conclusions about feedback-driven core formation. However, a minor tension exists in their timescales: Governato et al. emphasize that core formation starts early (bulk of stars form before z~1), while Onorbe et al. find the largest cores in systems that form stars late (z≲2), suggesting the timing of star formation relative to cusp-building mergers matters. Additionally, Onorbe et al. note that large cores are not ubiquitous—some ultrafaint dwarfs retain cusps—whereas Governato et al. report core formation in all systems above a stellar mass threshold, which may reflect differences in feedback prescriptions, halo mass ranges, or simulation resolution.

x.title: How supernova feedback turns dark matter cusps into cores
x.abstract: We propose and successfully test against new cosmological simulations a novel analytical description of the physical processes associated with the origin of cored dark matter density profiles. In the simulations, the potential in the central kiloparsec changes on sub‐dynamical time‐scales over the redshift interval 4 > z > 2, as repeated, energetic feedback generates large underdense bubbles of expanding gas from centrally concentrated bursts of star formation. The model demonstrates how fluctuations in the central potential irreversibly transfer energy into collisionless particles, thus generating a dark matter core. A supply of gas undergoing collapse and rapid expansion is therefore the essential ingredient. The framework, based on a novel impulsive approximation, breaks with the reliance on adiabatic approximations which are inappropriate in the rapidly changing limit. It shows that both outflows and galactic fountains can give rise to cusp flattening, even when only a few per cent of the baryons form stars. Dwarf galaxies maintain their core to the present time. The model suggests that constant density dark matter cores will be generated in systems of a wide mass range if central starbursts or active galactic nucleus phases are sufficiently frequent and energetic.

tag.main_claim: Pontzen and Governato show that repeated supernova feedback fluctuations irreversibly transfer energy into collisionless dark matter particles, transforming dark matter cusps into cores.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire mechanism presupposes that non-baryonic dark matter exists as collisionless particles that can receive energy from baryonic feedback processes. If P1 is rejected (as MOND does), there are no collisionless dark matter particles to heat and no cusps to flatten, making the claim meaningless.
tag.evidence_quote: The model demonstrates how fluctuations in the central potential irreversibly transfer energy into collisionless particles, thus generating a dark matter core.

y.title: From cusps to cores: a stochastic model
y.abstract: The cold dark matter model of structure formation faces apparent problems on galactic scales. Several threads point to excessive halo concentration, including central densities that rise too steeply with decreasing radius. Yet, random fluctuations in the gaseous component can ‘heat’ the centres of haloes, decreasing their densities. We present a theoretical model deriving this effect from first principles: stochastic variations in the gas density are converted into potential fluctuations that act on the dark matter; the associated force correlation function is calculated and the corresponding stochastic equation solved. Assuming a power-law spectrum of fluctuations with maximal and minimal cutoff scales, we derive the velocity dispersion imparted to the halo particles and the relevant relaxation time. We further perform numerical simulations, with fluctuations realized as a Gaussian random field, which confirm the formation of a core within a time-scale comparable to that derived analytically. Non-radial collective modes enhance the energy transport process that erases the cusp, though the parametrizations of the analytical model persist. In our model, the dominant contribution to the dynamical coupling driving the cusp-core transformation comes from the largest scale fluctuations. Yet, the efficiency of the transformation is independent of the value of the largest scale and depends weakly (linearly) on the power-law exponent; it effectively depends on two parameters: the gas mass fraction and the normalization of the power spectrum. This suggests that cusp-core transformations observed in hydrodynamic simulations of galaxy formation may be understood and parametrized in simple terms, the physical and numerical complexities of the various implementations notwithstanding.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that stochastic gas density fluctuations generate potential fluctuations that heat dark matter halo centers, transforming cusps into cores on timescales comparable to analytical predictions.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire mechanism presupposes that dark matter haloes exist and have cuspy profiles that need transformation (P1), and the force correlation function, velocity dispersion, and relaxation time calculations are all derived within Newtonian dynamics (P2). If dark matter haloes did not exist or if Newtonian dynamics broke down at low accelerations, the cusp-core problem and this solution would not arise.
tag.evidence_quote: stochastic variations in the gas density are converted into potential fluctuations that act on the dark matter; the associated force correlation function is calculated and the corresponding stochastic equation solved.

judge.conjunction: Studies have shown that repeated supernova-driven gas fluctuations irreversibly transfer energy into collisionless dark matter particles, transforming cusps into cores [x], and that this process can be derived from first principles as a stochastic effect in which gas density variations generate potential fluctuations that heat halo centers on timescales comparable to analytical predictions [y].
judge.notes: The conjunction is largely unproblematic: both papers operate within Framework P (Lambda-CDM), invoke the same physical mechanism (gas-induced potential fluctuations heating collisionless dark matter), and the 2016 paper appears to build directly on the 2012 result. One minor tension: paper x attributes the fluctuations specifically to repeated, energetic supernova feedback bursts, whereas paper y frames the driver more abstractly as stochastic gas density variations with a power-law spectrum, leaving open whether the specific astrophysical source of those fluctuations is always supernova feedback. A reviewer might also note that paper x validates the mechanism primarily through cosmological simulations, while paper y derives it analytically and confirms with idealized Gaussian random field simulations, so conflating the two lines of evidence without distinguishing their methodologies could overstate the convergence of results.

x.title: MOND theory
x.abstract: A general account of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) theory is given. I start with the basic tenets of MOND, which posit departure from standard dynamics in the limit of low acceleration — below an acceleration constant a0 — where dynamics become scale invariant. I list some of the salient predictions of these tenets. The special role of a0 and its significance are then discussed. In particular, I stress its coincidence with cosmologically relevant accelerations, which may point to MOND having deep interplay with cosmology. The deep-MOND limit and the consequences of its scale invariance are considered in some detail. There are many ways to achieve scale invariance of the equations of motion — guaranteed if the total action has a well-defined scaling dimension. The mere realization that this is enough to ensure MOND phenomenology opens a wide scope for constructing MOND theories. General aspects of MOND theories are then described, after which I list briefly presently known theories, both nonrelativistic and relativistic. With few exceptions, the construction of known, full-fledged theories follows the same rough pattern: they modify the gravitational action; hinge on a0; introduce, already at the level of the action, an interpolating function between the low and high accelerations; and they obey MOND requirements in the two opposite limits. These theories have much heuristic value as proofs of various concepts (e.g., that covariant MOND theories can be written with correct gravitational lensing). But, probably, none points to the final MOND theory. At best, they are effective theories of limited applicability. I argue that we have so far explored only a small corner of the space of possible MOND theories. I then outline several other promising approaches to constructing MOND theories that strive to obtain MOND as an effective theory from deeper concepts, for example, by modifying inertia and (or) gravity as a result of interactions with some omnipresent agent. These have made encouraging progress in various degrees, but have not yet resulted in full-fledged theories that can be applied to all systems and situations. Some of the presently known theories do enjoy a natural appearance of a cosmological-constant-like contribution that, furthermore, exhibits the observed connection with a0. However, none were shown to address fully the mass discrepancies in cosmology and structure formation that are otherwise explained by cosmological dark matter. This may well be due to our present ignorance of the true connections between MOND and cosmology. We have no clues as to whether and how MOND aspects enter nongravitational phenomena, but I discuss briefly some possibilities.

tag.main_claim: Milgrom reviews MOND theory and shows that its basic tenets—departure from standard dynamics below acceleration a0 and scale invariance in the deep-MOND limit—open a wide scope for constructing modified gravity theories that reproduce MOND phenomenology including correct gravitational lensing, though no complete theory yet addresses all cosmological mass discrepancies.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's entire theoretical program rests on MOND's core claims: that galaxy dynamics need no dark matter (Q1), that Newtonian dynamics break down below a0 (Q2), and that scaling relations follow from the modified force law (Q3). Rejecting any of these would eliminate the foundation on which the constructions and predictions described in the paper are built.
tag.evidence_quote: I start with the basic tenets of MOND, which posit departure from standard dynamics in the limit of low acceleration — below an acceleration constant a0 — where dynamics become scale invariant. I list some of the salient predictions of these tenets.

y.title: MOND laws of galactic dynamics
y.abstract: Modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) predicts a number of laws that galactic systems should obey irrespective of their complicated, haphazard and mostly unknowable histories – as Kepler's laws are obeyed by planetary systems. The main purpose of this work is to show how, and to what extent, these MOND laws follow from only the paradigm's basic tenets: departure from standard dynamics at accelerations a ≲ a0 and space–time scale invariance in the limit a ≪ a0. Such predictions will be shared by all MOND theories that embody these premises. This is important because we do not know which of the existing MOND theories, if any, is a step in the right direction. In the Newtonian dynamics plus dark matter paradigm, the validity of such clear-cut laws – which tightly constrain baryons, ‘dark matter’ and their mutual relations – is contrary to expectations.

tag.main_claim: Milgrom shows that MOND predicts clear-cut laws of galactic dynamics that follow directly from the paradigm's basic tenets—modified dynamics at low accelerations and space-time scale invariance—akin to how Kepler's laws follow from Newtonian gravity.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's claim that galactic dynamical laws follow from MOND tenets requires that galaxy dynamics be explained without dark matter (Q1), that Newtonian dynamics break down below a0 (Q2, explicitly cited as a basic tenet), and that scaling relations derive from the force law rather than from galaxy formation (Q3).
tag.evidence_quote: The main purpose of this work is to show how, and to what extent, these MOND laws follow from only the paradigm's basic tenets: departure from standard dynamics at accelerations a ≲ a0 and space–time scale invariance in the limit a ≪ a0.

judge.conjunction: Milgrom [x, y] demonstrates that MOND's basic tenets—departure from standard dynamics below the acceleration constant a0 and space-time scale invariance in the deep-MOND limit—not only yield clear-cut, Kepler-like laws of galactic dynamics that follow directly from these premises, but also open a wide scope for constructing modified gravity theories that reproduce MOND phenomenology including correct gravitational lensing, though no complete theory yet addresses all cosmological mass discrepancies.
judge.notes: Both papers are by the same author (Milgrom) and within the same framework (MOND), so the claims are complementary rather than conflicting. Minor concern: the 'basic tenets' are described slightly differently across the two claims—Claim X emphasizes scale invariance of the action/equations of motion, while Claim Y emphasizes space-time scale invariance—which are related but not identical formulations, so the literature-review writer should verify that the merged phrasing is precise enough. Additionally, the juxtaposition of strong predictive success (Kepler-like laws) with the acknowledged failure to address cosmological mass discrepancies could invite a reader to question the overall viability of the paradigm, though this is an internal tension within MOND rather than a contradiction between the two claims.

x.title: Breakdown of the Newton–Einstein Standard Gravity at Low Acceleration in Internal Dynamics of Wide Binary Stars
x.abstract: Abstract A gravitational anomaly is found at weak gravitational acceleration g N ≲ 10−9 m s−2 from analyses of the dynamics of wide binary stars selected from the Gaia DR3 database that have accurate distances, proper motions, and reliably inferred stellar masses. Implicit high-order multiplicities are required and the multiplicity fraction is calibrated so that binary internal motions agree statistically with Newtonian dynamics at a high enough acceleration of ≈10−8 m s−2. The observed sky-projected motions and separation are deprojected to the 3D relative velocity v and separation r through a Monte Carlo method, and a statistical relation between the Newtonian acceleration g N ≡ GM/r 2 (where M is the total mass of the binary system) and a kinematic acceleration g ≡ v 2/r is compared with the corresponding relation predicted by Newtonian dynamics. The empirical acceleration relation at ≲10−9 m s−2 systematically deviates from the Newtonian expectation. A gravitational anomaly parameter δ obs−newt between the observed acceleration at g N and the Newtonian prediction is measured to be: δ obs−newt = 0.034 ± 0.007 and 0.109 ± 0.013 at g N ≈ 10−8.91 and 10−10.15 m s−2, from the main sample of 26,615 wide binaries within 200 pc. These two deviations in the same direction represent a 10σ significance. The deviation represents a direct evidence for the breakdown of standard gravity at weak acceleration. At g N = 10−10.15 m s−2, the observed to Newton-predicted acceleration ratio is g obs / g pred = 10 2 δ obs − newt = 1.43 ± 0.06 . This systematic deviation agrees with the boost factor that the AQUAL theory predicts for kinematic accelerations in circular orbits under the Galactic external field.

tag.main_claim: Chae shows that wide binary stars exhibit a breakdown of Newtonian gravity at low accelerations (~10^-9 m/s^2), with observed accelerations exceeding Newtonian predictions by a factor consistent with AQUAL/MOND theory.
tag.dependence_explanation: The central claim that standard gravity breaks down at low accelerations directly requires Q2, which states that Newtonian dynamics fail below a characteristic acceleration a0. The paper's interpretation of the observed deviation as a fundamental gravity breakdown—and its agreement with AQUAL predictions—only makes sense if Newtonian dynamics are indeed modified at low accelerations.
tag.evidence_quote: The deviation represents a direct evidence for the breakdown of standard gravity at weak acceleration. At g N = 10 −10.15 m s−2, the observed to Newton-predicted acceleration ratio is g obs / g pred = 10 2 δ obs − newt = 1.43 ± 0.06 . This systematic deviation agrees with the boost factor that the AQUAL theory predicts for kinematic accelerations in circular orbits under the Galactic external field.

y.title: Measurements of the Low-acceleration Gravitational Anomaly from the Normalized Velocity Profile of Gaia Wide Binary Stars and Statistical Testing of Newtonian and Milgromian Theories
y.abstract: Abstract Low-acceleration gravitational anomaly is investigated with a new method of exploiting the normalized velocity profile v ˜ ≡ v p / v c of wide binary stars as a function of the normalized sky-projected radius s/r M, where v p is the sky-projected relative velocity between the pair, v c is the Newtonian circular velocity at the sky-projected separation s, and r M is the MOND radius. With a Monte Carlo method, Gaia observed binaries and their virtual Newtonian counterparts are probabilistically distributed on the s/r M versus v ˜ plane, and a logarithmic velocity ratio parameter Γ is measured in the bins of s/r M. With three samples of binaries covering a broad range in size, data quality, and implied fraction of hierarchical systems including a new sample of 6389 binaries selected with accurate distances and radial velocities, I find a unanimous systematic variation from the Newtonian flat line. With Γ = 0 at s/r M ≲ 0.15 or s ≲ 1 kau, I get Γ = 0.068 ± 0.015 (stat) − 0.015 + 0.024 (syst) for s/r M ≳ 0.7 or s ≳ 5 kau. The gravitational anomaly (i.e., acceleration boost) factor given by γ g = 102Γ is measured to be γ g = 1.37 − 0.09 + 0.10 (stat) − 0.09 + 0.16 (syst). With a reduced χ 2 test of Newtonian and Milgromian nonrelativistic theories, I find that Newtonian gravity is ruled out at 5.8σ ( χ ν 2 = 9.4 ) by the new sample (and 9.2σ by the largest sample used). The Milgromian AQUAL theory is acceptable with 0.7 ≲ χ ν 2 ≲ 3.1 . These results agree well with earlier results with the “acceleration-plane analysis” for a variety of samples and the “stacked velocity profile analysis” for a pure binary sample.

tag.main_claim: Chae (2024) shows that wide binary stars exhibit a gravitational anomaly at low accelerations consistent with Milgromian (MOND/AQUAL) dynamics and inconsistent with Newtonian gravity, ruling out Newtonian gravity at 5.8σ.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's central claim that Newtonian gravity is ruled out in favor of Milgromian dynamics directly depends on Q2, which posits that Newtonian dynamics break down below a characteristic acceleration a0. The entire analysis is structured around testing dynamics near the MOND radius and acceleration scale, and the claimed anomaly only makes sense if Q2 is true.
tag.evidence_quote: With a reduced χ 2 test of Newtonian and Milgromian nonrelativistic theories, I find that Newtonian gravity is ruled out at 5.8σ ( χ ν 2 = 9.4 ) by the new sample (and 9.2σ by the largest sample used). The Milgromian AQUAL theory is acceptable with 0.7 ≲ χ ν 2 ≲ 3.1 .

judge.conjunction: Analyses of Gaia wide binary stars have revealed a consistent gravitational anomaly at low accelerations, with observed accelerations exceeding Newtonian predictions by a factor of roughly 1.4 in a manner compatible with AQUAL/MOND expectations, thereby challenging the validity of Newtonian gravity in the low-acceleration regime [x,y].
judge.notes: Both papers are by the same author (Chae) and draw on overlapping Gaia DR3 datasets with similar methodologies, so they do not constitute fully independent confirmations. The reported boost factors differ slightly (1.43 ± 0.06 vs. 1.37 with larger systematic errors), and paper y notes AQUAL is only marginally acceptable (0.7 ≲ χ²ν ≲ 3.1), meaning MOND is not definitively favored over Newtonian gravity in an absolute sense. Both studies must contend with the systematic uncertainty of unresolved hierarchical multiples contaminating the binary samples, which remains the dominant alternative explanation. Additionally, both papers operate within Framework Q (MOND); if a reviewer requires consistency with Framework P (ΛCDM), these claims directly conflict with P2 (Newtonian dynamics hold at low accelerations), making the conjunction problematic in that broader theoretical context.

x.title: Rotation Curves of Ursa Major Galaxies in the Context of Modified Newtonian Dynamics
x.abstract: This is the third in a series of papers in which spiral galaxy rotation curves are considered in the context of Milgrom's modified dynamics (MOND). The present sample of 30 objects is drawn from a complete sample of galaxies in the Ursa Major cluster, with photometric data from Tully et al. and 21 cm line data from Verheijen. The galaxies are roughly all at the same distance (15 to 16 Mpc). The radio observations are made with the Westerbork Synthesis Array, which means that the linear resolution of all rotation curves is comparable. The greatest advantage of this sample is the existence of K '-band surface photometry for all galaxies; the near-infrared emission, being relatively free of the effects of dust absorption and less sensitive to recent star formation, is a more precise tracer of the mean radial distribution of the dominant stellar population. The predicted rotation curves are calculated from the K '-band surface photometry and the observed distribution of neutral hydrogen using the simple MOND prescription, in which the one adjustable parameter is the mass of the stellar disk or the implied mass-to-light ratio. The predicted rotation curves generally agree with the observed curves, and the mean M / L in the near-infrared is about 0.9 with a small dispersion. The fitted M / L in the B -band correlates with B - V color in the sense predicted by population synthesis models. Including earlier work, about 80 galaxy rotation curves are now well reproduced from the observed distribution of detectable matter using the MOND formula to calculate the gravitational acceleration; this lends considerable observational support to Milgrom's unconventional hypothesis.

tag.main_claim: Sanders shows that MOND reproduces the rotation curves of about 80 galaxies from the observed distribution of baryonic matter alone, with mass-to-light ratios consistent with stellar population synthesis predictions.

y.title: THINGS about MOND
y.abstract: We present an analysis of 12 high-resolution galactic rotation curves from The HI Nearby Galaxy Survey (THINGS) in the context of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND). These rotation curves were selected to be the most reliable for mass modelling, and they are the highest quality rotation curves currently available for a sample of galaxies spanning a wide range of luminosities. We fit the rotation curves with the “simple” and “standard” interpolating functions of MOND, and we find that the “simple” function yields better results. We also redetermine the value of a0, and find a median value very close to the one determined in previous studies, a0 = (1.22 ± 0.33) × 10-8 cm s-2. Leaving the distance as a free parameter within the uncertainty of its best independently determined value leads to excellent quality fits for 75% of the sample. Among the three exceptions, two are also known to give relatively poor fits in Newtonian dynamics plus dark matter. The remaining case (NGC 3198) presents some tension between the observations and the MOND fit, which might, however, be explained by the presence of non-circular motions, by a small distance, or by a value of a0 at the lower end of our best-fit interval, 0.9 × 10-8 cm s-2. The best-fit stellar M/L ratios are generally in remarkable agreement with the predictions of stellar population synthesis models. We also show that the narrow range of gravitational accelerations found to be generated by dark matter in galaxies is consistent with the narrow range of additional gravity predicted by MOND.

judge.conjunction: Studies of galaxy rotation curves have consistently shown that MOND reproduces observed kinematics from the baryonic mass distribution alone with mass-to-light ratios consistent with stellar population synthesis predictions, from Sanders's sample of approximately 80 Ursa Major galaxies [x] to the high-resolution THINGS survey confirming the 'simple' interpolating function and a consistent value of a0 [y].
judge.notes: Both papers operate within Framework Q (MOND), so their claims share a consistent theoretical background and the conjunction is largely unproblematic. The two studies differ in sample size and data quality: Sanders (1998) uses ~80 galaxies with moderate-resolution 21 cm data, while the THINGS paper (2010) examines 12 high-resolution rotation curves. The THINGS analysis finds that 25% of its sample (3/12, including NGC 3198) shows some tension with MOND fits, slightly qualifying the combined claim. Both papers converge on the 'simple' interpolating function and consistent M/L ratios, reinforcing rather than contradicting each other.
